stem: A 58-year-old man with hypertension has had a dry, nonproductive cough for 3 months. It began a few weeks after he started lisinopril. He has no wheeze, dyspnea, edema or orthopnea, and a chest x-ray is normal.
oneliner: 58M + dry cough 3 mo + began weeks after lisinopril + normal CXR, no wheeze or edema → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **No wheeze or dyspnea**; no variable airflow symptoms
whyNot.B: **No edema, orthopnea or dyspnea**; normal chest x-ray
whyNot.D: No heartburn or regurgitation; **cough began after the new drug**
whyNot.E: **Dry, not productive**, and the x-ray is normal

why: **Dry cough starting weeks after lisinopril** with a normal chest x-ray = bradykinin buildup from ACE inhibition.

stem: A 47-year-old woman has had two episodes of swelling of the lips, tongue and throat since starting enalapril 6 weeks ago. She has no itching or hives, no known allergies, and no family history of similar swelling.
oneliner: 47F + lip/tongue/throat swelling x2 + 6 wk on enalapril + no hives, no allergies, no family hx → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.B: **No family history**; onset only after starting the drug
whyNot.C: **No hives or itching**, no allergen exposure
whyNot.D: **No hives or pruritus**; swelling is deep in lips and tongue
whyNot.E: No rash or exposure; swelling is **deep, episodic and involves the tongue and throat**

why: **Recurrent lip/tongue swelling weeks after an ACE inhibitor** with no hives and no family history = bradykinin-mediated angioedema.

stem: A 55-year-old man with hypertension is brought in with severe headache, sweating and palpitations. Three days ago he ran out of his medicines and stopped both his diuretic and clonidine. Pulse is 118/min and blood pressure is 170/110 mm Hg. He has never had similar spells before, and his thyroid exam and temperature are normal.
oneliner: 55M + HTN, stopped clonidine and diuretic 3 d ago + headache + sweating + palpitations + BP 170/110 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Never had similar spells**; symptoms began only after stopping a drug
whyNot.B: **Normal thyroid exam and temperature**
whyNot.C: **BP 170/110** with a clear drug-stop trigger
whyNot.E: Stopping a diuretic alone does not cause a **sympathetic surge** with tachycardia

why: **Abrupt stop of clonidine** followed by headache, sweating, tachycardia and BP surge = rebound sympathetic overactivity.

stem: A 68-year-old woman has had new shortness of breath on exertion for 2 weeks. She has never smoked and has no history of lung disease. Her ophthalmologist started timolol eye drops for glaucoma 3 weeks ago. Lungs are clear on auscultation, and spirometry shows an FEV1 lower than her previous value.
oneliner: 68F + exertional dyspnea 2 wk + timolol drops 3 wk ago + clear lungs + FEV1 down → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Onset **follows the new eye drops**; no wheeze or atopy history
whyNot.C: **Reduced FEV1** means airflow limitation; no pleuritic pain or leg swelling
whyNot.D: Lungs are **clear**, no edema or orthopnea
whyNot.E: **Never smoked**; decline began right after the new drops

why: **Timolol drops** (nonselective beta blocker) then **new dyspnea with lower FEV1** and clear lungs = beta-2 blockade causing bronchoconstriction.

stem: A 34-year-old man is brought in after swallowing a large number of his metoprolol tablets. Pulse is 38/min and blood pressure is 70/40 mm Hg. Glucose is normal, and his pupils are normal. After an infusion of glucagon his heart rate and blood pressure rise.
oneliner: 34M + metoprolol tablets swallowed + HR 38 + BP 70/40 + improves with glucagon → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Glucagon-responsive picture after **metoprolol**, a beta blocker; no calcium channel blocker taken
whyNot.B: **No digoxin exposure**; no visual change or GI symptoms
whyNot.C: **No clonidine taken**; pupils are normal, no marked sedation
whyNot.D: **Normal pupils**, no secretions, no cholinergic signs

why: **Bradycardia and hypotension after metoprolol** that respond to glucagon (bypasses the blocked beta receptor) = beta-blocker overdose.

stem: A 62-year-old man with stable angina takes isosorbide mononitrate daily. Four hours ago he took a sildenafil tablet from a friend. He now develops chest pain and collapses. Blood pressure is 60/30 mm Hg and pulse is 104/min. The ECG shows sinus tachycardia and no heart block.
oneliner: 62M + angina on isosorbide + friend's sildenafil 4 h ago + collapse + BP 60/30 + sinus tach → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: ECG shows **sinus tachycardia with no block**
whyNot.B: **Normal rhythm** on ECG; no QT drug or long QT
whyNot.D: **Sinus rhythm at 104/min**, not an abrupt narrow-complex tachycardia
whyNot.E: Pulse is **104/min, not slow**; no beta blocker taken

why: **Nitrate plus a PDE-5 inhibitor** → excess cGMP and profound vasodilation → collapse with BP 60/30.

stem: A 71-year-old woman with heart failure takes digoxin and furosemide. Over the past two days she has had nausea, vomiting, loss of appetite and yellow-tinged vision. Last night she took extra digoxin tablets by mistake. Potassium is 7.2 mEq/L and creatinine is normal.
oneliner: 71F + HF on digoxin + extra doses + nausea/vomiting + yellow vision + K 7.2 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Creatinine is normal**; vision change and extra digoxin doses explain the high K
whyNot.C: **No adrenal disease**; K rose after a drug overdose, with visual symptoms
whyNot.D: Loop diuretics **lower** potassium, not raise it
whyNot.E: **Visual disturbance and K 7.2** do not fit infection

why: **Extra digoxin with GI upset, yellow vision and K 7.2** = Na/K-ATPase inhibition (hyperkalemia, visual and GI toxicity).

stem: A 60-year-old man with a hypertensive emergency has received a nitroprusside infusion for 48 hours. He becomes lethargic with rapid, labored breathing. His blood pressure is now 124/78 mm Hg. Arterial pH is 7.21 with a high anion gap and elevated lactate, and oxygen saturation by pulse oximetry is 99%.
oneliner: 60M + nitroprusside x48 h + lethargy + labored breathing + lactic acidosis, SpO2 99% → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No anemia or abdominal pain**; fits the nitroprusside timeline instead
whyNot.C: **No iron ingestion** or GI bleeding
whyNot.D: **Normal pulse oximetry reading and no chocolate-colored blood**; lactic acidosis points to blocked cellular respiration
whyNot.E: **No fire or heating source exposure**; infusion drug explains the picture

why: **Prolonged nitroprusside infusion** with **lactic acidosis and lethargy despite normal saturation** = cyanide blocking cytochrome oxidase.

stem: A 42-year-old woman with depression starts amitriptyline. One week later she reports constipation, difficulty passing urine and a dry mouth. Temperature is 37.0 C and pulse is 96/min. Her muscle tone and reflexes are normal and she has no agitation or sweating. Pelvic ultrasonography shows a distended bladder.
oneliner: 42F + depression, amitriptyline 1 wk + constipation + urinary retention + dry mouth, normal tone and reflexes → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.D: Anticholinergic adverse effects of a tricyclic antidepressant

whyNot.A: **Normal tone and reflexes**, no agitation, sweating or clonus
whyNot.B: Would cause **hyponatremia and concentrated urine**, not retention
whyNot.C: **Onset in a week after a new drug**; no cold intolerance or bradycardia
whyNot.E: **No opioid taken**; dry mouth and retention began with the new drug

why: **Constipation, urinary retention and dry mouth after a tricyclic** = muscarinic receptor blockade.

stem: A 66-year-old man has burning, shooting pain in both feet from diabetic neuropathy. His physician started nortriptyline 10 days ago. He now has trouble passing urine and has a full feeling in the lower abdomen. Prostate exam showed a normal-sized gland 6 months ago, and he has had no urinary symptoms before.
oneliner: 66M + neuropathic foot pain on nortriptyline 10 d + new urinary retention + prostate normal 6 mo ago → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No prior urinary symptoms and normal prostate** a few months ago
whyNot.B: **Not on carbamazepine**; retention follows a tricyclic
whyNot.C: No agitation, clonus, hyperthermia or diarrhea
whyNot.D: Neuropathy is longstanding but **retention began only after the new drug**

why: **New retention 10 days after nortriptyline** in a man with no prior voiding problems = antimuscarinic detrusor effect.

stem: A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes has had difficulty starting his urine stream, dribbling and a feeling that his bladder never empties for the past week. The symptoms started after he began taking diphenhydramine nightly for seasonal allergies. His glucose is well controlled and he had no urinary complaints before. Prostate exam is normal in size.
oneliner: 64M + diabetes + hesitancy, dribbling, incomplete emptying 1 wk + started nightly diphenhydramine, prostate normal → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Prostate is normal in size** and symptoms began only after the antihistamine
whyNot.B: **Glucose is well controlled** and symptoms began within a week of the new drug
whyNot.D: Not on a diuretic; symptoms are **hesitancy and retention, not urgency**
whyNot.E: **No dysuria or fever**; no infectious clues

why: **Hesitancy and incomplete emptying after nightly diphenhydramine** with a normal prostate = antimuscarinic effect on the bladder.

stem: A 60-year-old man smokes and has diabetes. For 3 months he has had pressure behind the sternum when climbing stairs, lasting about 5 minutes and relieved by rest. The pain is not related to meals or breathing and cannot be reproduced by pressing on the chest. Cardiac exam is normal.
oneliner: 60M + smoker + diabetes + exertional substernal pressure 5 min, relieved by rest + not reproducible, normal cardiac exam → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Not related to meals**; exertional and relieved by rest
whyNot.C: **Normal cardiac exam**, no murmur
whyNot.D: **Cannot be reproduced by palpation**; exertional pattern
whyNot.E: **Not pleuritic or positional**; no rub

why: **Exertional chest pressure relieved by rest** in a smoker with diabetes = fixed atherosclerotic coronary narrowing (stable angina).

stem: A 22-year-old man has yellow nodules over both Achilles tendons and the knuckles. His father had a myocardial infarction at age 41. LDL cholesterol is 340 mg/dL, triglycerides are 120 mg/dL, and TSH and urinalysis are normal.
oneliner: 22M + Achilles and knuckle tendon xanthomas + father MI at 41 + LDL 340, TG 120, normal TSH → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Triglycerides are normal**; LDL is the elevated fraction
whyNot.B: LDL would be **very low**, not 340
whyNot.C: **Normal TSH**
whyNot.E: **Normal urinalysis**; no proteinuria or edema

why: **Tendon xanthomas, premature family MI and isolated very high LDL** = defective LDL receptor pathway.

stem: A 24-year-old woman starts a high-dose B-vitamin supplement she bought to lower her cholesterol. Twenty minutes after the first dose she has warm, red flushing of the face and neck with itching. She has no hives, lip swelling or wheeze, and her blood pressure is 118/72 mm Hg.
oneliner: 24F + new high-dose B-vitamin for cholesterol + flush and itch of face/neck 20 min after dose + no hives, wheeze or swelling → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.B: **No hives, swelling, wheeze or hypotension**
whyNot.C: **No diarrhea or wheeze**; flush follows each dose of the supplement
whyNot.D: Age 24, with flush **timed to the supplement**
whyNot.E: **No hives, abdominal pain or prior episodes**; reaction is dose-related

why: **Flushing and itch minutes after high-dose vitamin B3** with no airway or BP involvement = prostaglandin-mediated vasodilation.

stem: A 22-year-old man having knee surgery receives halothane and succinylcholine. Thirty minutes later his temperature is 40.6 C, pulse is 142/min and his jaw and limbs become rigid. End-tidal CO2 is rising and urine is dark brown. He takes no regular medicines.
oneliner: 22M + halothane and succinylcholine → fever 40.6 + generalized rigidity + HR 142 + rising end-tidal CO2 + dark urine → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No antipsychotic**; onset within minutes of anesthesia
whyNot.B: **No serotonergic drug**; rigidity with rising CO2 right after anesthetic
whyNot.C: **Abrupt onset during surgery** with rigidity and dark urine, no infection source
whyNot.E: **No thyroid disease**; sudden rigidity after anesthetic

why: **Fever, rigidity and hypercarbia right after halothane and succinylcholine** = ryanodine receptor–mediated sustained Ca2+ release in muscle.

stem: A 38-year-old man receives succinylcholine for intubation before an appendectomy that lasts 30 minutes. Forty-five minutes after the injection he still cannot breathe or move on his own, although he follows commands by blinking. Temperature is 37.0 C, muscles are flaccid, and potassium is 4.2 mEq/L. His mother had similar prolonged paralysis after surgery.
oneliner: 38M + succinylcholine for intubation → still paralyzed and apneic at 45 min + flaccid, awake + normal temp and K + mother had same → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Flaccid, normal temperature**; no rigidity or hypercarbia
whyNot.B: **No weakness before surgery**; paralysis lasts only after a depolarizing blocker
whyNot.D: **Potassium is normal**
whyNot.E: Would cause **sedation**, not flaccid paralysis in an awake patient

why: **Prolonged paralysis after succinylcholine with a positive family history** = slow hydrolysis of the drug by plasma cholinesterase.

stem: A 70-year-old woman is breathing weakly 20 minutes after abdominal surgery. She received vecuronium during the case and no succinylcholine. Stimulating the ulnar nerve produces weak, fading twitches of the thumb. Temperature is normal and muscles are flaccid.
oneliner: 70F + post-op weak breathing + vecuronium given + fading twitches on ulnar nerve stimulation + flaccid, afebrile → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Vecuronium, not succinylcholine, was given**
whyNot.C: **Afebrile and flaccid**, no rigidity
whyNot.D: **No weakness before surgery**; the block follows a nondepolarizing agent
whyNot.E: Nerve stimulation shows **fading muscle block**, not just sedation with slow breathing

why: **Weak post-op breathing after vecuronium with fading twitches** = competitive ACh receptor block not yet cleared.

stem: A 45-year-old woman with myasthenia gravis recently had her pyridostigmine dose raised. She now has worsening weakness and shortness of breath, with abdominal cramps, diarrhea and drooling. Pulse is 48/min, pupils are small, and her tongue and thigh muscles twitch. Bowel sounds are hyperactive.
oneliner: 45F + myasthenia on pyridostigmine dose raised + weakness + dyspnea + HR 48 + small pupils + fasciculations + hyperactive bowel sounds → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Would show **dilated or normal pupils, normal heart rate and no secretions or cramps**
whyNot.B: **Proximal weakness that improves with repeated effort, with dry mouth**; no cholinergic excess
whyNot.C: **No ascending areflexia**; fasciculations and **bradycardia with cramps** follow a dose increase
whyNot.D: Causes **dilated pupils, dry mouth and constipation**, the opposite of this picture

why: **Excess pyridostigmine** causing weakness plus bradycardia, miosis, cramps, drooling and fasciculations = acetylcholine overload.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought in after snorting a white powder 20 minutes ago. He is euphoric and sweating, with palpitations. Pulse is 128/min, blood pressure is 172/104 mm Hg, pupils are dilated and the nasal mucosa is red and irritated. The rush has been short-lived.
oneliner: 17M + snorted white powder 20 min ago + euphoria, sweating + HR 128 + BP 172/104 + dilated pupils + red nasal mucosa → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Dilated pupils with tachycardia and hypertension**, not miosis and bradycardia
whyNot.B: **Inhaled powder with irritated nasal mucosa** and abrupt short rush
whyNot.D: **Euphoric**, not tremulous with hallucinations; no recent heavy drinking
whyNot.E: **No nystagmus, aggression or rigidity**

why: **Intranasal powder, brief euphoria, tachycardia, hypertension, mydriasis and irritated nasal mucosa** = blocked catecholamine reuptake.

stem: A 24-year-old man collapses and dies at a party. At autopsy the heart is structurally normal, the coronary arteries are patent, and there is no intracranial hemorrhage. Urine toxicology is positive for benzoylecgonine.
oneliner: 24M + sudden death at party + normal heart, patent coronaries, no brain bleed + urine benzoylecgonine → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.C: Acute myocardial infarction from coronary thrombosis

whyNot.B: Heart is **structurally normal at autopsy**
whyNot.C: **Coronaries are patent**
whyNot.D: **No intracranial hemorrhage**
whyNot.E: Toxicology shows **benzoylecgonine**, a cocaine metabolite, not opiates

why: **Benzoylecgonine with a structurally normal heart and patent coronaries** = sudden death from catecholamine-driven arrhythmia.

stem: A 26-year-old man who takes dextroamphetamine tablets daily is brought in restless and irritable. He has a fine tremor, pulse 118/min, blood pressure 158/96 mm Hg, respirations 24/min and dilated pupils. Temperature is 37.2 C. He has no clonus, no history of alcohol use and no goiter.
oneliner: 26M + daily amphetamine tablets + restless, irritable + tremor + HR 118 + BP 158/96 + RR 24 + mydriasis, no clonus or goiter → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: He takes **amphetamine tablets**, not a snorted or smoked powder
whyNot.C: **No alcohol history**; pupils dilated with no hallucinations or seizures
whyNot.D: **No goiter**; onset follows drug use
whyNot.E: **No clonus**, hyperreflexia or fever

why: **Known amphetamine use with restlessness, tremor, tachycardia, hypertension and mydriasis** = sympathetic overstimulation.

stem: A 17-year-old boy is brought from a party. He stares blankly, is rigid, and then becomes suddenly violent, seemingly unaware of pain. Pulse is 110/min and blood pressure is 160/100 mm Hg. Examination shows vertical nystagmus and normal-sized pupils.
oneliner: 17M + party + blank stare + rigid + sudden violence, no pain response + vertical nystagmus + HR 110, BP 160/100 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Vertical nystagmus and rigidity with blank stare** are not features; pupils are dilated in stimulant use
whyNot.B: **Agitated and hypertensive**, not sedated with pinpoint pupils
whyNot.C: Would cause **sedation without violence or nystagmus**
whyNot.D: **Vertical nystagmus and numbness to pain** are not features; pupils would be dilated

why: **Blank stare, violence with analgesia and vertical nystagmus** = NMDA receptor antagonist intoxication.

stem: A 15-year-old boy has had 6 months of headaches, confusion, clumsiness with frequent falls and falling grades. He has a wide-based, unsteady gait and a red rash around the nose and mouth. His breath has a sharp chemical odor and blood alcohol is zero. Urine toxicology for common drugs is negative.
oneliner: 15M + 6 mo headaches, confusion, falls, grades dropping + ataxic gait + perioral rash + chemical-smelling breath, BAC 0 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Blood alcohol is zero**; breath odor is chemical, not ethanol
whyNot.C: Would cause **tachycardia and hypertension**; urine toxicology is negative
whyNot.D: **Negative urine toxicology**, no weight loss or dental decay; cerebellar ataxia is prominent
whyNot.E: **No aggression or vertical nystagmus**; negative toxicology

why: **Perioral rash, chemical breath, ataxia and cognitive decline in a teen with negative toxicology** = chronic solvent (toluene) inhalation.

stem: A 78-year-old woman is on postoperative day 3 after hip surgery and is receiving morphine through a patient-controlled pump. She is now difficult to arouse. Respirations are 6/min, pupils are pinpoint and equal, and temperature is 36.9 C. Creatinine is 1.8 mg/dL (it was 0.9 before surgery). Glucose is 110 mg/dL and there is no focal weakness.
oneliner: 78F + POD3 hip surgery on morphine PCA + RR 6 + pinpoint pupils + creatinine 1.8 + afebrile, glucose normal → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Afebrile**, no hypotension or leukocytosis described
whyNot.B: **No focal weakness**; pupils equal and pinpoint
whyNot.C: **Glucose is 110 mg/dL**
whyNot.D: Would not cause **pinpoint pupils and RR 6** to this degree; she is on morphine

answer: Opioid overdose (morphine toxicity with renal impairment)
why: **Morphine PCA, RR 6 and pinpoint pupils with renal impairment** = accumulation of active morphine metabolites.

stem: A 29-year-old man is found unresponsive after taking a large dose of methadone. Respirations are 4/min and pupils are pinpoint. He wakes and breathes normally after an injection of naloxone. Ninety minutes later he becomes drowsy again, with respirations of 6/min and pinpoint pupils. He has had no new drug exposure in the hospital.
oneliner: 29M + methadone overdose, woke with naloxone → drowsy again at 90 min + RR 6 + pinpoint pupils → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

options.A: Opioid overdose (recurrent sedation as naloxone wears off)

whyNot.B: **No rash, wheeze or hypotension**; the picture returns to the original one
whyNot.C: He **responded to naloxone** and has pinpoint pupils
whyNot.D: **No seizure** witnessed; pinpoint pupils and slow respirations
whyNot.E: He **woke fully** after naloxone; pupils are pinpoint, not fixed or dilated

why: **Response to naloxone then relapse at 90 min** = naloxone wears off before the long-acting opioid.

stem: A 20-month-old girl with diarrhea was given three adult-strength capsules of an over-the-counter antidiarrheal by her father. She is now pale and unresponsive, with respirations of 6/min and a distended abdomen with absent bowel sounds. She is afebrile, pupils are small and skin is moist.
oneliner: 20-month-old F + three adult OTC antidiarrhea capsules + pale, unresponsive + RR 6 + small pupils + distended abdomen, absent bowel sounds → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Small pupils and moist skin**, not dilated pupils and dry skin
whyNot.B: **Afebrile** and onset right after the capsules
whyNot.C: **No colicky pain or currant-jelly stool**; respiratory depression and miosis
whyNot.E: Causes **dilated pupils and descending weakness**, not miosis and sedation

why: **Antidiarrheal overdose with miosis, respiratory depression and ileus** = mu-opioid agonism (loperamide).

stem: A 2-year-old girl is found with her grandmother's empty bottle of 60 diazepam tablets. She is drowsy but arousable. Pulse is 110/min, respirations are 20/min, blood pressure is normal, pupils are normal in size and the ECG is normal.
oneliner: 2F + empty bottle of 60 diazepam + drowsy but arousable + RR 20, normal pupils, normal ECG → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Drug taken was **diazepam**; early presentation with drowsiness
whyNot.B: **Normal ECG, pupils and no seizures** or hypotension
whyNot.D: **Normal pupils and normal respiratory rate**
whyNot.E: **No secretions, miosis or bradycardia**

why: **Diazepam ingestion with drowsiness but preserved breathing and normal vitals** = benzodiazepine (GABA-A) CNS depression.

stem: A 32-year-old woman is found stuporous after taking a large number of her phenobarbital tablets. Respirations are 6/min and shallow. Chest x-ray is clear and there was no vomiting. Room-air arterial blood gas: pH 7.21, PaCO2 70 mm Hg, PaO2 55 mm Hg, HCO3 27 mEq/L; calculated A-a gradient is 7 mm Hg.
oneliner: 32F + phenobarbital tablets swallowed + stuporous + RR 6 + clear CXR + pH 7.21, PaCO2 70, PaO2 55, A-a gradient 7 → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Clear chest x-ray and normal A-a gradient**
whyNot.C: **Normal A-a gradient** and hypercapnia, not hypocapnia
whyNot.D: **Clear lungs on x-ray and normal A-a gradient**
whyNot.E: Would cause **respiratory alkalosis and tachypnea**, not hypoventilation

why: **Phenobarbital ingestion with RR 6, hypercapnia and a normal A-a gradient** = hypoventilation from CNS depression.

stem: A 41-year-old woman is found semicomatose next to an empty bottle of her old secobarbital sleeping pills. Respirations are 8/min, blood pressure is 88/54 mm Hg and temperature is 35.2 C. Pupils are midsize and reactive, reflexes are reduced, and there are no needle marks. Her breath has no alcohol odor, and the ECG is normal.
oneliner: 41F + empty secobarbital bottle + semicomatose + RR 8 + BP 88/54 + T 35.2 + midsize pupils, no needle marks, normal ECG → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Would cause **tachypnea, tinnitus and fever**, not slow breathing and hypothermia
whyNot.B: **Midsize pupils and no needle marks**; pills were a sedative
whyNot.C: **Normal ECG**, no dilated pupils or seizures
whyNot.E: **No alcohol odor** on the breath

why: **Coma, slow breathing, hypotension and hypothermia** after an empty **secobarbital** bottle, with midsize pupils = barbiturate overdose.

stem: A 32-year-old man with schizophrenia had his haloperidol dose raised 3 days ago. He is now confused, with temperature 40.1 C, pulse 124/min and sweating. Muscles are stiff throughout, and there is no tremor or clonus. Creatine kinase is 1,500 U/L.
oneliner: 32M + schizophrenia, haloperidol increased 3 d ago + T 40.1 + confusion + generalized lead-pipe rigidity + CK 1,500, no clonus → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: **No anesthetic exposure**; onset over days after a dose increase
whyNot.C: **No fever, autonomic instability or high CK**
whyNot.D: **No clonus or hyperreflexia**; slow-onset rigidity after antipsychotic
whyNot.E: Causes **involuntary choreiform movements**, not fever and rigidity

why: **Dopamine antagonist dose increase with fever, lead-pipe rigidity, confusion and high CK** = hypothalamic and basal ganglia D2 blockade.

stem: A 38-year-old man has taken fluoxetine for depression for 3 weeks. Two days ago he began a tryptophan supplement for sleep. He now has agitation, sweating, diarrhea and tremor. Temperature is 38.8 C, and he has diffuse hyperreflexia and inducible ankle clonus.
oneliner: 38M + fluoxetine 3 wk + started tryptophan 2 d ago + agitation + sweating + diarrhea + T 38.8 + hyperreflexia, clonus → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Hyperreflexia and clonus**, rapid onset, and no antipsychotic
whyNot.B: **Sweating and diarrhea**, not dry skin and ileus
whyNot.D: **No anesthetic exposure**; MH causes rigidity, not clonus
whyNot.E: **Clonus and hyperreflexia after adding a serotonin precursor**; no goiter or eye signs

why: **SSRI plus tryptophan with clonus, hyperreflexia, diarrhea and fever** = excess serotonergic stimulation.

stem: A 52-year-old man who takes phenelzine for depression develops a pounding occipital headache an hour after a dinner of aged cheese and red wine. Blood pressure is 230/145 mm Hg and pulse is 112/min. His neck is supple, there are no focal deficits, and he has never had episodic spells.
oneliner: 52M + phenelzine + aged cheese and red wine → pounding headache + BP 230/145 + HR 112, supple neck, no prior spells → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No prior episodic spells**; clear dietary trigger on an MAO inhibitor
whyNot.B: **No clonus, hyperreflexia or diarrhea**
whyNot.C: BP is **230/145 with no tearing, rhinorrhea or ptosis**
whyNot.D: **Supple neck**, no focal deficits

why: **MAOI plus aged cheese and wine with severe headache and BP 230/145** = tyramine-induced norepinephrine surge.

stem: A 45-year-old man was started on haloperidol 10 days ago for a psychotic episode. He now moves slowly, has a masked face and a shuffling gait, and has increased tone in all four limbs. Temperature is 37.0 C, he is alert, and creatine kinase and heart rate are normal. He has no clonus.
oneliner: 45M + haloperidol 10 d ago + slow movements + masked face + shuffling gait + symmetric rigidity + afebrile, normal CK → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Symmetric** signs that began **days after the antipsychotic**; Parkinson disease is gradual and asymmetric
whyNot.C: **Afebrile, alert, normal CK** and normal heart rate
whyNot.D: **No clonus**, fever, diarrhea or agitation
whyNot.E: Causes **involuntary movements** after months, not early rigidity

why: **Symmetric bradykinesia and rigidity days after a D2 blocker, without fever or high CK** = reversible dopamine blockade.

stem: A 35-year-old man has taken phenytoin for epilepsy for 8 years with no problems. A week ago his physician added cimetidine for a duodenal ulcer. He now has drowsiness, unsteady gait and horizontal nystagmus. He has no limb weakness, no alcohol use and no confusion, and his eye movements are otherwise full.
oneliner: 35M + epilepsy stable on phenytoin 8 y + cimetidine added 1 wk ago + drowsy + ataxia + nystagmus, no weakness, no alcohol → ?

whyNot.E: **No dermatitis, diarrhea or dementia**

why: **Isoniazid without pyridoxine in an alcohol drinker, then new distal sensory neuropathy** = B6 depletion.

stem: A 36-year-old woman with Graves disease has taken propylthiouracil for 6 months. She now has fever of 39.2 C, chills and a severely painful throat with ulcerating tonsils. WBC is 1,800/mm3 with an absolute neutrophil count of 100/mm3. She has no rash or purpura.
oneliner: 36F + Graves on PTU 6 mo + fever 39.2 + ulcerating sore throat + WBC 1,800, ANC 100 + no rash → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **No purpura or rash**; ANC is profoundly low
whyNot.B: **Neutropenia and ulcerating pharyngitis** are not features; she is on treatment
whyNot.C: **ANC is 100**, not the leukocytosis of a normal infection
whyNot.D: Would show **lymphocytosis with atypical lymphocytes**, not neutropenia

why: **Thionamide use with fever, ulcerating pharyngitis and ANC 100** = drug-induced agranulocytosis.

stem: A 58-year-old obese woman with type 2 diabetes and hypertension is found comatose at home. For an hour beforehand she complained of palpitations, sweating and double vision. Fingerstick glucose is 38 mg/dL. Her purse contains bottles of glipizide, acarbose and lisinopril. Serum insulin and C-peptide are both elevated. Sodium, potassium and blood pressure are normal.
oneliner: 58F + type 2 DM, HTN + palpitations, sweating, diplopia → coma + glucose 38 + purse with glipizide, acarbose, lisinopril + high insulin and high C-peptide → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Acarbose alone **does not cause severe hypoglycemia**; insulin and C-peptide are high
whyNot.C: **C-peptide is elevated**, so insulin is endogenous
whyNot.D: Causes at most **a mild glucose drop**, not high insulin and C-peptide
whyNot.E: **Normal sodium, potassium and blood pressure**

why: **Glipizide with hypoglycemia and high insulin plus high C-peptide** = sulfonylurea-driven beta-cell insulin release.

stem: A 1-day-old boy has respiratory distress and has passed no urine in the first 24 hours. His mother took lisinopril for hypertension throughout pregnancy, and ultrasonography at 30 weeks showed too little amniotic fluid. He has a poorly ossified skull and low-set ears. Renal ultrasonography shows small kidneys of normal shape, and chest x-ray shows small lungs.
oneliner: 1-day-old M + respiratory distress + anuria + mother on lisinopril all pregnancy + oligohydramnios + small normal-shaped kidneys, small lungs, poorly ossified skull → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Mother took lisinopril**; no nasal hypoplasia or stippled epiphyses
whyNot.B: **No thymic, cardiac or ear-canal malformations**; renal failure with oligohydramnios
whyNot.D: **Kidneys are small and normal in shape**, not enlarged and cystic
whyNot.E: **No cardiac malformation**; fetal renal failure

why: **Lisinopril in pregnancy with oligohydramnios, fetal renal failure, pulmonary hypoplasia and skull hypoplasia** = lack of angiotensin II effect on the fetal kidney.

stem: A 1-day-old girl is small for gestational age and has a head circumference below the 3rd percentile. She has short palpebral fissures, a smooth philtrum and a thin upper lip. A systolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border. Her mother drank vodka daily throughout the pregnancy and takes no medicines.
oneliner: 1-day-old F + small + microcephaly + short palpebral fissures + smooth philtrum + thin upper lip + VSD murmur + mother drank vodka daily, no medicines → ?
ask: What is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: **Mother takes no anticonvulsant**; no nail or distal phalanx hypoplasia
whyNot.B: **No upslanting fissures, epicanthal folds or single palmar crease**
whyNot.C: **No hypocalcemia, cleft palate or absent thymus**
whyNot.E: **No cataracts, deafness or maternal rash**

why: **Daily maternal alcohol with microcephaly, short palpebral fissures, smooth philtrum, thin upper lip and a VSD** = fetal alcohol syndrome.

stem: A 1-day-old boy has a soft, fluid-filled lumbosacral sac that contains neural tissue, with weak legs. His mother has epilepsy and took valproic acid throughout pregnancy without folic acid. She does not have diabetes, did not take warfarin, and had no rash or fever in pregnancy.
oneliner: 1-day-old M + lumbosacral myelomeningocele + weak legs + mother on valproic acid all pregnancy, no folic acid, no diabetes → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely cause?

whyNot.A: **Mother took valproate, not phenytoin**; no nail hypoplasia or cleft lip
whyNot.B: **Mother is not diabetic**; defect is a neural tube defect
whyNot.C: **No warfarin exposure**; no nasal hypoplasia or stippled epiphyses
whyNot.D: **No rash or fever in pregnancy**, no cataracts or deafness

why: **Valproate in the first trimester with a myelomeningocele** = neural tube defect from valproate-induced folate interference.
